# CII Hails GST Reforms As Transition To Trust-Based Governance

  

Date:  2026-11-01 06:00:42

([MENAFN](https://menafn.com/1111898393/CII-Hails-GST-Reforms-As-Transition-To-Trust-Based-Governance)- IANS) New Delhi, Nov 1 (IANS) Apex [business](https://menafn.com/1111898393/CII-Hails-GST-Reforms-As-Transition-To-Trust-Based-Governance#) chamber CII said on Sunday that the GST Council's landmark decisions on decriminalisation and rationalisation of enforcement powers of tax officials were among the most significant institutional reforms in India's transition towards trust-based economic governance.
CII said the importance of the GST reforms marks a fundamental shift towards more proportionate enforcement, greater predictability, and confidence in legitimate business activity, while retaining strong safeguards against deliberate fraud and evasion.

“Reaching agreement on such fundamental changes is a substantial achievement of cooperative federalism. It demonstrates the willingness of the Centre and states to reconsider established regulatory practices in favour of greater trust in legitimate enterprise," CII Director General Chandrajit Banerjee said in a statement.

The GST Council's decisions encompass the removal of arrest powers through the omission of Section 69 of the CGST Act, a fivefold increase in the monetary threshold for prosecution from Rs 1 crore to Rs 5 crore, narrowing of specified offences under Section 132, and rationalisation of imprisonment provisions, including greater judicial discretion in sentencing.

These decisions represent a fundamental recalibration of GST enforcement while retaining criminal prosecution for serious cases of deliberate fraud and evasion. They recognise that genuine commercial disputes, procedural lapses and deliberate wrongdoing must be treated differently. For businesses, particularly MSMEs and first-generation entrepreneurs, the significance lies in reducing the uncertainty, reputational risks, legal costs and management disruption associated with disproportionate criminal consequences, the chamber noted.

"The importance of this reform is not simply that certain enforcement powers are being withdrawn. It is that the GST Council has recognised that effective tax administration need not depend on the threat of criminal sanctions. This is one of the most consequential steps towards trust-based governance in recent years, particularly given the reach of GST across virtually every sector of the economy," CII said.

CII further noted that the developments since the Council meeting have reinforced this direction. CBIC's circulars issued on October 26 address practical concerns relating to registration, notices, and adjudication, including the need to substantiate allegations of fraud with evidence, provide greater clarity in tax notices and ensure reasoned adjudication. These instructions address longstanding concerns of industry, where uncertainty over interpretation, documentation requirements and allegations of wrongdoing can impose substantial costs even before disputes are resolved.

Together with the Council's decisions on faster refunds, input tax credit, and compliance simplification, these measures can improve working capital efficiency, reduce avoidable disputes and make tax administration more predictable. Their full impact will depend on consistent implementation across jurisdictions, the statement added.

# Trump loses final round: Judge throws out his $10bn Epstein-linked defamation case against Wall Street Journal

## A birthday card, a $10bn lawsuit and two rulings from the same judge. Trump sued a day after the story ran, hoping to silence the Wall Street Journal. Instead, a Miami courtroom has now closed the book on his case for good.

A US federal judge has permanently ended Donald Trump’s defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal and its owner, Rupert Murdoch. It closes a case that began with a single news story about a birthday card sent to Jeffrey Epstein.

Judge Darrin Gayles of the US District Court in Miami threw out the case “with prejudice.” That phrase matters. It means Trump cannot bring the same claim again in the lower court.

Gayles said Trump failed to show “actual malice.” This is the legal bar a public figure must clear to win a defamation case in the United States. The judge called the claims of malice vague and conclusory. Also, he said some were inconsistent with the article itself.

He went further. He suggested Trump’s lawyers had tried to manufacture flaws in the paper’s investigation. In his words, Trump was grasping at straws.

The ruling is the second dismissal in this case. The first came in April. This one is final in the trial court.

The standard comes from a 1964 Supreme Court case, New York Times v. Sullivan. It protects the press when it reports on public officials and public figures.

To win, a public figure must prove two things. First, the statement was false. Second, the publisher knew it was false, or showed reckless disregard for the truth.

A mistake is not enough. Even sloppy reporting is not enough. The plaintiff must show the publisher had real doubts and went ahead anyway. That is a hard test to meet. It is meant to be hard.

Trump has long said he wants this standard changed. The ruling shows it is still in force.

## The story that started it all

On July 17, 2025, The Wall Street Journal published an exclusive. It described a birthday note sent to Jeffrey Epstein for his 50th birthday in 2003.

The note was part of a book of letters from friends and well-known people. The British socialite Ghislaine Maxwell reportedly collected them. Maxwell is now serving a 20-year prison sentence for her role in Epstein’s sex-trafficking scheme.

The note attributed to Trump had typed text. A hand-drawn outline of a curvy woman framed the text. Trump’s signature sat near the bottom of the drawing.

A copy of the letter was later released by the House Oversight Committee. Democrats on the committee made it public in September 2025.

## Trump’s denial

Trump denied writing the words. He denied signing the note. He denied drawing the picture.

On Truth Social, he said the paper had printed a fake letter. He called the coverage false, malicious and defamatory.

The Journal had asked him for comment before publishing. It printed his denial in the article. Judge Gayles pointed to this in his April ruling. He said it let readers decide for themselves.

## The lawsuit

Trump sued on July 18, 2025. That was one day after the story ran. He filed in federal court in Miami.

He asked for more than $10 billion in damages. And, he said the story caused overwhelming financial and reputational harm.

The defendants were many. They included Dow Jones, the paper’s publisher, and [News](https://www.thestatesman.com/world/trump-loses-final-round-judge-throws-out-his-10bn-epstein-linked-defamation-case-against-wall-street-journal-1503657554.html#) Corp, its parent company. Murdoch was named personally. So was News Corp chief executive Robert Thomson. Two Journal reporters who worked on the story were also named.

The complaint said the paper acted knowingly and recklessly. It said the defendants published false and disparaging statements.

## The first dismissal

Judge Gayles dismissed the case on April 13, 2026. He ruled that Trump had not plausibly alleged actual malice.

The judge noted how the paper handled the story. Reporters contacted Trump before publication. They also reached out to the Justice Department and the FBI. The judge treated this as normal journalistic practice.

That ruling was “without prejudice.” This gave Trump a way back in. He had until April 27 to file an amended complaint.

Dow Jones welcomed the decision. A spokesperson said the company stood behind the accuracy and rigor of its reporting.

Trump’s team said it would follow the judge’s guidance. It promised to refile what it called a powerhouse lawsuit.

## The refiled complaint

Trump filed an amended complaint on May 27, 2026. It tried to fix the weakness the judge had named.

The new filing leaned on a few points. It said the Journal was reckless because it did not show how its reporters got and checked the letter. Also, it questioned how deep the reporting went.

It made a claim about Murdoch too. That said Trump told Murdoch the letter was fake. It said Murdoch replied that he would handle it. Trump read this as a sign the story would not run.

The complaint also cited Maxwell. It said she told federal officials, under penalty of perjury, that she had no memory of Trump sending a birthday note.

Judge Gayles was not persuaded. His final ruling said the malice claims were conclusory. He also said many of the allegations had little to do with what the defendants knew when they published.

## What Trump argued

Trump had a further argument. He said the case should go on because the Journal could not prove the note was real beyond doubt. This held even after the House committee released a copy.

The law does not work that way in a case like this. The burden sits with the plaintiff. Trump had to show the paper knew or strongly suspected the letter was false. The court found he did not.

## No deposition for Murdoch

The dismissal has one practical effect. Murdoch will not have to sit for a deposition about the birthday book and the paper’s reporting.

Had the case moved to discovery, both sides could have demanded documents and testimony. Newsroom records and reporter communications might have come into play. The early dismissals closed that door.

## Epstein background

The case sits on top of a larger story. Jeffrey Epstein was a wealthy financier with ties to powerful people in politics, business and academia.

In 2008, he was convicted in Florida of soliciting a minor for sex. He served 13 months in jail.

In 2019, he faced federal sex-trafficking charges in New York. He was found dead in his jail cell before trial. His death was ruled a suicide.

Legal advocates say his victims may number in the hundreds.

Trump and Epstein socialised in the past. In 2025, Trump said he cut ties after Epstein “stole” female staff from the Mar-a-Lago resort.

Critics have kept asking about the nature of the friendship. The Journal story added fuel at a tense time.

## The political backdrop

The article landed while the Trump administration was under heavy pressure. Critics said it had held back files on the Epstein case. They noted that officials had promised transparency.

This helps explain why the story drew so much attention. It also helps explain why Trump reacted so quickly. The lawsuit came within a day.
